newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrcia rand bears bale out but prepare to return.
newsitem.headline: SAfrcia rand bears bale out but prepare to return.

text.p: A sharp rally in the South African rand, which started late Tuesday, was running out of steam on Wednesday as bears prepared their return.
Dealers said speculators who were long dollars got burned in the last 24 hours and were forced to bale out of positions as the first decisive exporter demand for rand emerged in weeks.
That triggered a series of stop-loss dollar sales that boosted the rand to 4.64 from 4.70 early on Wednesday.

"There were an awful lot of people who got themselves very long of dollars and who were stopped out in the last couple of trading sessions," said Chris Tinker, chief treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank in London.

"There's been a bit of a shakeout, and I would now expect people to start looking to buy dollars on the dips...Sentiment is very much that the trend depreciation in the currency is still as much in place as it ever was," he said.
By Wednesday afternoon, demand for the U.S. unit from local importers and offshore banks taking up fresh positions had pulled the rand back to 4.67.

Charles Jonker, forex economist at Absa Bank, said some rand bears may have also been spooked in part this week by growing talk of a rate hike and speculation about South Africa seeking a $2 billion International Monetary Fund (IMF) loan.

"I don't think anything has changed. But there is a lot of emphasis on an upward move in interest rates, and the market's perception is we may be getting closer to IMF finance and using 15 billion rand of offshore credit lines," he said.
"That creates the threat of the Reserve Bank having bigger intervention powers, and speculators don't want to go long in dollars if there is a chance of the Bank becoming stronger," Jonker said.

Comments by Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals last week may have defused some of the immediate uncertainty in the market, although his statement that exchange controls would remain for up to five years were generally disappointing, analysts said.
His renewed emphasis on making the fight against inflation top priority suggested continued high interest rates, whatever the currency trend, which leant some solace to the rand.
A further kick-up in the daily money market shortage to nearly 10 billion rand on Tuesday also fuelled talk of a rate hike sooner rather than later.
Nevertheless, Jonker saw the latest moves as a correction rather than a trend change.

Further rand losses were expected in coming days because South Africa's fundamentals have not changed, economists said. They said concerns over uncertain policy and low reserves would prompt speculators to re-establish bearish rand positions.
In the absence of a fresh capital injection from the IMF, the problems that have beset the rand since February could soon return to haunt the market, economists said.

Reserves stand at a precarious four weeks import cover and the balance of payments situation is only expected to improve slowly despite the rand's near 30-percent fall against the dollar this year, which should boost exports and curb imports.
"Every time we've seen a corrective phase like this, people getting long of rand for any period of time tend to find themselves hurt," Tinker said.
